info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 11.3: AI-Assisted Alignment and Gloss Generation.

name.text: 01 Question: Entering Step 3: AI-Assisted Text Alignment

questiontext.text: What distinctive capability do neural AI models bring to text alignment that simple length formulas lack?

generalfeedback.text: AI models bring semantic and grammatical understanding to alignment, offering powerful assistance that must be audited against human expertise.

answer.text: Deep semantic and grammatical understanding of multilingual syntax, vocabulary, and context.

feedback.text: Correct. Unlike length-based formulas, AI models understand grammatical structure and can recognize relationships across complex reordered translations.

answer.text: The ability to print physical books without using electricity.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AI models run computationally in digital environments.

answer.text: A legal guarantee that all generated text is 100% free of errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AI models frequently make subtle errors and require rigorous human auditing.

answer.text: Automatic deletion of all historical French and Latin vocabulary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AI models analyze multilingual historical vocabulary.

name.text: 02 Question: How AI Differs from Deterministic Algorithms

questiontext.text: What is a primary operational difference between deterministic tools and neural AI models?

generalfeedback.text: While deterministic tools rely on fixed length calculations, AI models predict linguistic patterns and require supervision against hallucinations.

answer.text: Deterministic tools follow fixed mathematical formulas without guessing, while AI models predict probable linguistic patterns.

feedback.text: Correct. Deterministic tools never hallucinate but struggle with shifted syntax; AI models understand syntax but can invent non-standard facts.

answer.text: Deterministic tools only work on mobile phones, while AI models only run on supercomputers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both tools run on standard laptop computers in VS Code.

answer.text: Deterministic tools require internet access, while AI models require paper index cards.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Deterministic scripts run offline locally.

answer.text: AI models are completely incapable of processing English text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AI models excel at processing English and multilingual text.

name.text: 03 Question: AI Inside Visual Studio Code

questiontext.text: Why is working with AI assistants directly inside VS Code advantageous for digital editors?

generalfeedback.text: Working with AI directly inside VS Code allows you to review suggestions in split editor diff views without leaving your workspace.

answer.text: It allows editors to review suggestions in side-by-side diff views with direct file context, avoiding external copy-pasting.

feedback.text: Correct. Embedded AI tools inspect open workspace files directly and allow students to accept or reject diffs cleanly.

answer.text: It automatically locks the laptop keyboard so students cannot type.

feedback.text: Incorrect. VS Code empowers students to edit and control their text.

answer.text: It sends all student grades directly to social media.

feedback.text: Incorrect. VS Code is a secure, private development environment.

answer.text: It deletes the user's local Git repository to save storage space.

feedback.text: Incorrect. VS Code integrates with Git to preserve version control.

name.text: 04 Question: Prompt Engineering for Structured Alignment

questiontext.text: Why must editors provide structured system prompts rather than casual chat requests when generating TEI markup?

generalfeedback.text: Structured prompts with explicit roles, input boundaries, and output formats force AI models to generate clean, valid TEI markup.

answer.text: To force the AI to produce well-formed XML data and prevent conversational filler or unrequested formatting.

feedback.text: Correct. Structured prompts specify role, exact input boundaries, schema rules, and expected XML tags.

answer.text: Because AI models become angry if you speak to them casually.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models do not have feelings; structured prompts ensure machine-readable data.

answer.text: Because casual prompts cause the computer's fan to stop spinning.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Prompt structure affects text generation, not cooling hardware.

answer.text: Because TEI guidelines require prompts to be written in rhyming verse.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Prompts are written in clear, concise technical English.

name.text: 05 Question: Prompting for Four-Line Leipzig Glosses

questiontext.text: What critical formatting constraint must be emphasized when prompting an AI for Leipzig glosses?

generalfeedback.text: Prompting for Leipzig glosses requires demanding four synchronized tiers, standard uppercase tags, and preserved historical surface orthography.

answer.text: Demanding that every word in Line 1 correspond to exactly one vertical column in Line 2 and Line 3.

feedback.text: Correct. Forcing strict column synchronization prevents horizontal shifting and maintains morpheme-by-morpheme alignment.

answer.text: Demanding that all four lines be translated into modern Spanish.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Leipzig glosses analyze the primary source language using standard grammatical tags and an English translation.

answer.text: Instructing the AI to delete all vowels from the historical text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical spelling must be fully preserved.

answer.text: Requiring that every sentence be exactly one hundred words long.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Sentence lengths vary according to the historical witness.

name.text: 06 Question: Negative Constraints: What to Forbid

questiontext.text: What is the function of negative constraints in prompt engineering for digital editions?

generalfeedback.text: Negative constraints prevent the AI from modernizing historical spelling, hallucinating classical roots, or violating Leipzig punctuation rules.

answer.text: They establish explicit boundaries that forbid the AI from modernizing spelling, hallucinating roots, or skipping words.

feedback.text: Correct. Negative constraints act like guardrails, preventing models from committing common generative errors.

answer.text: They prevent students from asking questions in classroom discussions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Negative constraints apply to AI prompts, not human students.

answer.text: They force the computer to shut down if an error occurs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Constraints guide text generation within the AI model.

answer.text: They delete negative numbers from financial spreadsheets.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Negative constraints are prompt instructions that forbid specific behaviors.

name.text: 07 Question: AI Failure Mode 1: Silent Modernization

questiontext.text: What is "silent modernization" in AI-assisted textual editing?

generalfeedback.text: AI models naturally bias toward modern spelling; editors must audit Line 1 to ensure historical orthography was not silently altered.

answer.text: When an AI model automatically and unnoticed alters historical orthography into contemporary standard spelling in Line 1.

feedback.text: Correct. AI models naturally bias toward modern web spelling, frequently smoothing over archaic spellings unless audited by an editor.

answer.text: When an author purchases a new laptop without telling the instructor.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Silent modernization refers to unauthorized alteration of historical text.

answer.text: When a manuscript fades over centuries due to sunlight exposure.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is physical degradation, not editorial modernization.

answer.text: When an XML parser changes all font sizes to twelve points.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It refers to spelling alterations in the text stream.

name.text: 08 Question: AI Failure Mode 2: The Portmanteau Confusion (Rule 2)

questiontext.text: How do AI models commonly violate Leipzig Rule 2 in Line 3 of an interlinear gloss?

generalfeedback.text: AI models often use hyphens instead of periods for fused grammatical features, violating Leipzig Rule 2.

answer.text: They use hyphens instead of periods for fused grammatical categories (e.g. writing speak-3-SG-PST instead of speak-3SG.PST).

feedback.text: Correct. Hyphens imply physical morpheme cuts; periods must be used when multiple categories belong to an indivisible ending.

answer.text: They replace all words with exclamation marks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The error is punctuation confusion between hyphens and periods.

answer.text: They write all grammatical labels in lowercase cursive font.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AI models usually use uppercase, but misapply hyphens.

answer.text: They delete Line 3 entirely and refuse to write it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models generate Line 3 but frequently violate Rule 2 punctuation.

name.text: 09 Question: AI Failure Mode 3: Hallucinated Grammatical Tags

questiontext.text: What should an editor do when an AI model proposes an unfamiliar uppercase tag in Line 3?

generalfeedback.text: AI models occasionally invent plausible but non-standard grammatical abbreviations, requiring human verification against standard Leipzig lists.

answer.text: Verify the abbreviation against the official Leipzig Glossing Rules list and replace it if it is non-standard.

feedback.text: Correct. AI models occasionally invent plausible-sounding but non-existent tags; human verification against official lists is essential.

answer.text: Assume the AI is smarter than all human linguists and accept the tag without checking.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly editing requires empirical verification, not blind trust.

answer.text: Delete the entire TEI document and drop out of university.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Catching and correcting AI mistakes is the core learning objective.

answer.text: Change the tag to a random emoji symbol.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly XML avoids informal symbols.

name.text: 10 Question: AI Failure Mode 4: Word Order and Pronoun Enclisis

questiontext.text: Why do inverted pronouns and clitics in French (such as dit-il or donnez-moi) challenge AI word alignment?

generalfeedback.text: Inverted pronouns, clitics, and irregular word orders frequently cause AI models to drop tokens or shift alignment columns.

answer.text: They alter standard word order and attach to verbs, causing models to drop pronouns or shift alignment columns.

feedback.text: Correct. Non-linear attachment and clitic inversion frequently cause generative models to lose column synchronization.

answer.text: Because French pronouns were outlawed during the French Revolution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pronouns remained in active use in revolutionary decrees.

answer.text: Because pronouns have no grammatical meaning in Romance languages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pronouns carry essential person, number, and case information.

answer.text: Because clitics cannot be typed on a standard computer keyboard.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Clitics are standard alphabetic characters.

name.text: 11 Question: The Three-Way Comparative Audit

questiontext.text: What are the three components compared in Friday's three-way comparative audit?

generalfeedback.text: The three-way comparative audit compares manual, deterministic, and AI-assisted outputs side by side to reveal the unique profile of each method.

answer.text: Version A (Tuesday Manual), Version B (Wednesday Deterministic), and Version C (Friday AI).

feedback.text: Correct. Comparing human baseline, mathematical algorithm, and neural model side by side reveals the unique strengths and limits of each approach.

answer.text: English, Spanish, and Italian print editions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The audit compares three computational methods applied to the student's primary witness.

answer.text: Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The files are TEI XML documents in the course repository.

answer.text: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner menus.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The audit evaluates textual alignment data.

name.text: 12 Question: What to Watch For: AI on Ace's 1791 French Decree

questiontext.text: When a long source sentence is translated as two target sentences, what can an AI aligner do that a length formula cannot?

generalfeedback.text: AI models can often recognize 1:2 splits by meaning, but every link and every Line 1 spelling still needs checking.

answer.text: It can see that both target sentences carry the meaning of one source sentence and link them 1:2.

feedback.text: Correct. The AI reads meaning across sentences, so it can propose a 1:2 link; you still check it.

answer.text: It can count the characters in each sentence exactly, which a length formula does only roughly.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A length formula counts characters exactly; that is its whole method.

answer.text: It can guarantee the historical spelling stays unchanged, which a length formula cannot promise.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AI models often modernize spelling; that is why Line 1 needs auditing.

answer.text: It can merge the two target sentences into one, so that a 1:1 link is always possible to make.

feedback.text: Incorrect. An aligner links sentences; it should not rewrite your target text.

name.text: 13 Question: What to Watch For: AI on Andromeda's 1752 Treaty

questiontext.text: What failure should Andromeda look for when an AI glosses the 1752 treaty?

generalfeedback.text: Check that the AI's glosses of formal treaty language are accurate and that its roots stay in plain English.

answer.text: Made-up Latin roots in Line 3 for archaic English spellings that need plain English roots.

feedback.text: Correct. AI models sometimes invent classical roots; Line 3 should use plain English roots.

answer.text: Missing article numbers in Line 1, because AI models delete every numeral from old texts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AI models do not routinely delete numerals; check Line 1 anyway.

answer.text: French glosses in Line 3, because AI models assume every treaty was written in French.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There is no such general tendency; the treaty is in English.

answer.text: Reversed word order in Line 4, because AI models read colonial English from right to left.

feedback.text: Incorrect. English is read left to right by people and models alike.

name.text: 14 Question: What to Watch For: AI on Olyvia's Maud Lewis Letters

questiontext.text: Why should Olyvia reject an AI's grammatical corrections in Line 1 of a Maud Lewis gloss?

generalfeedback.text: Protect the authentic voice of personal correspondence from AI over-correction.

answer.text: Line 1 records what Lewis wrote, so changing her grammar erases her voice from the edition.

feedback.text: Correct. Line 1 is the witness; corrections belong in the regularized text, not here.

answer.text: Line 1 is reserved for the French translation, so English corrections belong in Line 2.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Line 1 is the original text; the free translation is Line 4.

answer.text: Line 1 is generated by the aligner, so manual edits will be overwritten on the next run.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Line 1 comes from your transcription, not from the aligner.

answer.text: Line 1 must match the dictionary exactly, so the AI's version is always the correct one.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Line 1 must match the witness, not a dictionary.

name.text: 15 Question: Measuring AI Performance: A Three-Way Scorecard

questiontext.text: According to our three-way evaluation scorecard, what is a primary trade-off of neural AI models compared to manual editing?

generalfeedback.text: A comparative scorecard documents precision, speed, depth, and orthographic fidelity across all three alignment approaches.

answer.text: AI is dramatically faster and grammatically capable, but has lower orthographic fidelity due to modern spelling biases.

feedback.text: Correct. AI models process text in seconds but require vigilant auditing to prevent silent modernization.

answer.text: AI models are completely free of all errors and require zero human checking.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AI models frequently make subtle errors.

answer.text: Manual editing is ten times faster than running a computer algorithm.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manual editing is slow and deliberate.

answer.text: Deterministic tools produce more hallucinations than generative AI models.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Deterministic tools follow fixed formulas and never hallucinate.

name.text: 17 Question: Synthesizing Reconciled Leipzig Glosses

questiontext.text: What verification step is essential before finalizing gloss_reconciled.xml?

generalfeedback.text: The reconciled gloss file delivers three verified, publication-ready Leipzig glosses that combine historical accuracy with linguistic precision.

answer.text: Checking Line 1 letter-by-letter against the high-resolution facsimile image to guarantee authentic historical spelling.

feedback.text: Correct. Checking the digital image ensures that no automated modernization or OCR slips survived into the publication-ready gloss.

answer.text: Deleting all quotation marks from Line 4.

name.text: 18 Question: TEI Header Attribution for AI Assistance

questiontext.text: How is AI assistance ethically and transparently recorded in a TEI XML document?

generalfeedback.text: Transparent TEI header documentation explicitly records AI assistance, detailing which suggestions were adopted and who verified the text.

answer.text: By adding a <change> element in <revisionDesc> with @resp="#ai" detailing which suggestions were adopted and verified.

answer.text: By hiding all references to computers so readers think the editor is a genius.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hiding AI contributions violates academic integrity.

answer.text: By deleting the <teiHeader> entirely from the document.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The teiHeader is the mandatory cataloguing core of any TEI edition.

answer.text: By sending an anonymous letter to the Text Encoding Initiative.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Attribution is recorded directly within the document metadata.

name.text: 19 Question: Validating Reconciled XML in VS Code

questiontext.text: Which command-line utility is run in the VS Code terminal to verify that reconciled alignment XML has zero well-formedness errors?

generalfeedback.text: Always run xmllint and editor validation checks to ensure reconciled alignment files are well-formed and schema-compliant.

answer.text: xmllint --noout

feedback.text: Correct. xmllint --noout parses the file and reports any syntax errors without cluttering the screen with text output.

answer.text: git push --force

answer.text: rm -rf /
